newsitem.title: USA: Conn. heat wave raises brownout concern -Northeast.
newsitem.headline: Conn. heat wave raises brownout concern -Northeast.

text.p: A withering heat wave has increased the possibility of a brownout and prompted the New England power grid to issue its first-ever "power watch" advisory, a Northeast Utilities spokesman said Thursday.
"So far, with the steps that we've taken, we're managing load," Northeast spokesman Tom Shiel told Reuters.

"Right now, we don't anticipate (a voltage reduction)," he said. "If the system stays as it is, it won't happen. But if we do lose another unit or transmission line, then it's not out of the realm of possibility."

Shiel said three major generating units in New England had gone offline: Salem Harbor 4 in Salem, Mass. (400 megawatts); Montville 6 in Montville, Conn. (400 MW); and Manchester 11 in Providence, R.I. (140 MW).

He said Northeast's Montville 6 unit developed a tube leak early Thursday morning, and that the problem could take one or two days to fix. "We have to wait for the boiler to cool down to get in to assess the problem and repair, and then bring it back on line."
The fact that three units are down places a strain on the rest of the system, Shiel said. "It cuts down on the number of contingencies that we have."
He said the power watch advisory signals that the New England situation is "very serious."
"Because of the anticipated high demand for power today -- we expect it to be somewhere around Monday or Tuesday's load -- we went into the power watch."

"A power watch is issued when electricity demand is high, and there is a possible need to reduce system voltage or implement other measures to safeguard the six=state region's electricity system. We ask customers to turn off unnecessary appliances and lights."
Shiel projected demand in Connecticut to peak around 5,800 MW on Thursday. The all-time record was set on Tuesday, at 6,017 MW, he said.
"Hopefully, we won't get that high, (but) it is a distinct possibility. We're hoping that people will take conservation measures."
